scores.values_concern: Crushing into food must be clearly distinguished from covert administration, which needs the person's agreement or a formal capacity-based process.
scores.accuracy_concern: Serrano Santos 2016 error rates (57.3% vs 30.8%) come from a small observational study and need checking against full text; 'no tablet should be split' overstates, since scored tablets are designed to be halved; crushing usually makes use off-licence, which should be stated accurately.
scores.sharpen: Open with one concrete example (a crushed modified-release tablet can release the whole dose at once) and say that crushing with the person's agreement is different from hiding medicine in food.

scores.accuracy_concern: The 413 of 1,116 figure is cited to the Beers-criteria paper; the incidence paper is Parekh 2018 BJCP. The Discharge Medicines Service is England-only and must not be implied for Scotland; discharge supply length varies and must not be given as one figure.
scores.sharpen: Lead with the three questions in nation-neutral wording and move service-specific facts to the LinkedIn version so the post holds in Scotland as well as England.

scores.accuracy_concern: The 12-month reduction was about half a dosing time per day (a modest effect), and falls were higher in the intervention arm (IRR 2.20); the post must not imply simplification improved outcomes, and residential aged care in Australia differs from home care.
scores.sharpen: Make the claim about what to count (dosing times as treatment burden) and present SIMPLER as showing feasibility with an unexplained falls signal, not as support for the recommendation.

scores.accuracy_concern: Verify that OPERAM reported a reduction in inappropriate prescribing as an outcome before the opening says 'cut'; the 86 in 100 figure is the proportion with inappropriate prescribing in the intervention arm, not a reduction, and the visual must not imply otherwise.
scores.sharpen: Close with one specific test readers can apply to the next deprescribing trial, such as whether the outcome measured was one patients value.

scores.accuracy_concern: Graves 1997 is a small, retrospective, single-clinic US study from 1997; 'for most medicines a stop can be reversed' needs qualifying for drugs with withdrawal effects or where restarting carries risk.
scores.sharpen: Keep the four-question card and rely less on the 1997 percentages, so it stands as public decision support clearly distinct from C06-09 and C06-17.

scores.accuracy_concern: The survey measured hypothetical willingness conditional on a doctor saying stopping was possible; the prescriber-reluctance premise needs a primary source, not Reeve's introduction; the adjusted odds ratio must not become 'times more likely'.
scores.sharpen: Make the conditional the point: willingness depended on the doctor raising it, so the practical move is for the prescriber to offer the option.

scores.accuracy_concern: Verify NICE NG5 wording on recording reasons for changes; the claim that medicines stopped in hospital are restarted after discharge has no identified source and should be dropped if none is found.
scores.sharpen: Add the receiving side: GPs and pharmacists can query any stop without a reason, and patients can ask for the reason to be written on the letter.

scores.accuracy_concern: Residual drug in used patches varies by product and should be described as 'a substantial amount' unless a specific figure is sourced; MHRA advice is on gov.uk pages that may not be openable here, so pair it with SPCs or published studies.
scores.sharpen: Add what to watch for (unusual drowsiness, slow or shallow breathing) and what to do, so carers know the warning sign as well as the three checks.

scores.accuracy_concern: The 26 in 100 headline comes from an old, small, retrospective VA study; inferring 'one change at a time' from an association with number of drugs stopped is weak; the D-PRESCRIBE withdrawal-symptom figure needs verifying.
scores.sharpen: If kept, merge with C06-05 as its practitioner version, or reframe around the specific drug classes that need tapering, using current sources.

scores.values_concern: The title 'a future the person may not have' reads as fatalistic; frame the review around the person's current goals rather than a shortened life.
scores.accuracy_concern: Kutner 2015 did not formally show noninferiority on 60-day mortality, so stopping must not be called proven safe; the Morin 2017 figures (30.3% to 47.2%; 15.8% on a statin) need checking; Swedish and US data may not reflect UK practice.
scores.sharpen: Open with the rise to about 47 in 100 taking ten or more medicines in the last month of life, and check against C19 and C07 candidates before selection.

scores.accuracy_concern: 'Common' covers 1 in 100 to 1 in 10, so 'up to 1 in 10' is only the upper bound; check the Knapp 2004 sample and figures; participants were reading hypothetical information, so the result shows how the words are read, not what people later did.
scores.sharpen: Close with a translation the reader can use at the kitchen table: 'common' means at most 10 in 100 people, and often fewer.

scores.accuracy_concern: Kesselheim 2014 is a US observational study reporting odds ratios, which must not become 'times more likely'; the UK claim about changing manufacturers between dispensings needs a source.
scores.sharpen: Give a UK-relevant example (the same generic from a different manufacturer) and keep the single practical check on the label.

scores.accuracy_concern: PRIME 'medication-related harm' included non-serious events and harm linked with non-adherence, so explain what the 37 in 100 counts; 85% of predictions were by doctors with under 5 years' experience, so 'whatever their experience' is weakly supported.
scores.sharpen: Say what counted as harm and how many needed healthcare, and close with a named follow-up route such as a community pharmacy check after discharge.

scores.accuracy_concern: Small 1999 trial (93 people) with attrition; the restart figure the headline depends on is only in the full text; the relative hazard must not be converted to absolute risk; overlaps C01 falls candidates and E071.
scores.sharpen: Anchor on current guidance (World Falls Guidelines, STOPPFall) and use Campbell only as a supporting example, or move the idea to C01.

scores.accuracy_concern: Tam 2005 figures need checking; the claim that hospital-supplied medicines are missing from GP records needs a UK source; tie the St John's wort interaction to a named source.
scores.sharpen: Lead with the most surprising example (beta-blocker eye drops can slow the heart, or a six-monthly bone injection that will not be in the bag) to strengthen the opening.

scores.accuracy_concern: Verify the QRD template wording; the claim that the imbalance leads people to stop useful medicines has no direct source and must be marked as a concern; the drug facts box trials were US general-population studies.
scores.sharpen: Run as a pair with C06-11 or merge them, and give one real worked benefit figure so readers see what answer they are asking for.
Add one worked example (a new blood pressure tablet: the goal, a check in a few weeks, stop if dizzy on standing) so the four questions feel concrete.

scores.accuracy_concern: Absolute differences are small (about 14 versus 7 in 1,000 at 90 days), so do not imply the cascade is very common; the 'possible third drug' step on the visual should be labelled illustrative.
scores.sharpen: Give the absolute figures in the post and close with the alternatives (lower the dose, switch the drug, or reconsider the need for it) rather than only 'reconsider the first drug'.

scores.accuracy_concern: Check the MHRA 2019 wording on which body weight to use and which patient groups it covers; some SPCs now allow eGFR for some drugs, so limit 'wrong number' to drugs whose dosing is based on creatinine clearance.
scores.sharpen: Name the triggers precisely (age 75 or over, low body weight or muscle mass, a DOAC or narrow-margin drug) so readers know when to calculate.

scores.accuracy_concern: Lertxundi 2017 figures (almost a third of admissions, 4-day longer stay, higher mortality) are observational and need checking; domperidone is often the preferred anti-sickness drug, so avoid implying all anti-sickness drugs are unsafe.
scores.sharpen: Add the safe alternative the ward can use and a line on planning doses when the person is nil by mouth before surgery.

scores.accuracy_concern: Sick day guidance has limited evidence and Think Kidneys warned of harms; the medicine lists differ between cards and SGLT2 inhibitors appear only on newer versions; most sources are web pages that may not be openable.
scores.sharpen: Lead with the restart instruction as the overlooked point, and restrict the medicine list to the current Scottish card.

scores.accuracy_concern: EMPOWER enrolled long-term benzodiazepine users taking them for sleep or anxiety, so 'sleeping tablets' is loose; stopping was measured through pharmacy renewals; both trials were in Quebec.
scores.sharpen: Name the medicine group accurately and add one line on what the booklet contained, so readers know what to ask for.

scores.accuracy_concern: The NICE 'a third to a half' figure dates from 2009 and older data; the claim that escalating doses on paper causes harm needs a source or should be dropped.
scores.sharpen: Make it specific to older people: include swallowing, dexterity, eyesight and timing as reasons, and give one no-blame question verbatim.

scores.accuracy_concern: The mortality difference was unexpected and not the primary outcome, so do not headline it; the 65 or over threshold applied only to US Black and Hispanic participants; verify NICE NG238 wording on aspirin.
scores.sharpen: Keep the two-column distinction as the core and give serious bleeding as natural frequencies (about 38 versus 28 in 1,000 over about 5 years).

scores.accuracy_concern: Lipska 2015 uses US NHANES data from 2001 to 2010 and shows potential overtreatment, not measured low blood sugars; a low HbA1c can also reflect anaemia or altered red cell turnover; the hypoglycaemia to falls link needs a source.
scores.sharpen: Add a UK source for targets in frailty and one question families can ask: how many low sugars have there been, and is the dose still right?

scores.accuracy_concern: Check which NICE guideline (NG5 or NG67) covers compliance aids and its wording; RPS 2013 is older guidance; the dexterity claim is unsourced.
scores.sharpen: Reconcile explicitly with E169 and open with the decision question, then give the branch most people miss (a pack does not help someone who doubts the medicine).

scores.accuracy_concern: The trial was in healthy volunteers after 8 weeks of treatment; the claim that step-down succeeds more often than stopping lacks trial support and should be phrased as guideline advice.
scores.sharpen: Say plainly that some people need long-term acid tablets and should not stop without advice, and give the rebound duration seen in the trial.

scores.accuracy_concern: Separation intervals for levothyroxine vary between sources (30 to 60 minutes before breakfast; 2 to 4 hours from calcium or iron), so quote the SPC wording and advise checking personal timings with a pharmacist.
scores.sharpen: Lead with the common real combination, a thyroid tablet and calcium taken together at breakfast, as a single concrete case.

scores.accuracy_concern: Qualitative interviews with 23 professionals report their accounts, not how often reviews exclude patients; the post must say so.
scores.sharpen: Keep the framing on workload and systems rather than individual GPs, and close with the three questions so it reads as a request.

scores.accuracy_concern: Verify START version 3 wording for laxatives with regular opioids and anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation; avoid repeating bone-protection examples (E095, E097).
scores.sharpen: Open with one concrete omission and the claim that a review judged by the number of drugs removed will miss it.

scores.accuracy_concern: Admission outcomes were secondary; kidney injury admissions did not show a clear difference; check whether gains persisted after the incentives ended before implying a lasting effect.
scores.sharpen: Open with the three design features (a few named combinations, lists of patients, paid time to review) and add the post-incentive finding if it can be sourced.

scores.accuracy_concern: Rate ratios from a nested case-control design; absolute risk is low (about 7 per 10,000 person-years overall); must not imply ibuprofen with only one of these drugs is shown safe.
scores.sharpen: Give the absolute context in the post and name what to use instead (paracetamol for most people, or ask the pharmacist).

allocation_reason: 30 of 32 candidates score 36 or more with no disqualifying flag (C06-09 duplicates C06-05; C06-14 scores 35), and well over 14 of them are distinct, well-evidenced and useful, so the category merits the maximum. Note: the weights as given sum to 11, so the true maximum is 55, not 50.
balance_note: Top 14 by rank: 4 practitioners (C06-18, C06-04, C06-13, C06-19), 5 public (C06-29, C06-15, C06-17, C06-20, C06-32), 5 both (C06-11, C06-22, C06-08, C06-25, C06-01): well balanced, and mostly teaching, explanation or good care rather than complaint. Avoid selecting overlapping pairs together without distinct angles: C06-11 and C06-16 (leaflets), C06-02 and C06-13 (PRIME discharge harm), C06-05 and C06-17 (planning stops), C06-21 and C06-32 (kidney-risk drug classes). Check cross-category overlap before finalising: C06-22 with C11 sleep, C06-24 and C06-25 with C07, C06-10 with C19, C06-20 with C15, C06-28 with C04, C06-08 with C10.
